proofs.proof_tex:
By \(\mathrm{def{:}observed\text{-}block\text{-}means}\), \(\overline Y_l^{\mathrm{obs}}\) is a finite sum of coordinates of the observed vector \(Y^{\mathrm{obs}}\), divided by the positive integer \(r_l=|B_l|\); positivity follows from \(\mathrm{ass{:}partition}\).  It is therefore measurable with respect to \(D=(Z,Y^{\mathrm{obs}})\).  If \(A_l=1\), then every coordinate of \(Z\) in \(B_l\) equals one.  By \(\mathrm{ass{:}block\text{-}exposure}\), \(e_i(Z)=a\) for every \(i\in B_l\), and consistency in the definition of \(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}\) gives
\[
 \overline Y_l^{\mathrm{obs}}
 ={1\over r_l}\sum_{i\in B_l}Y_i(e_i(Z))
 ={1\over r_l}\sum_{i\in B_l}Y_i(a)=\mu_l(a).
\]
The same argument with every assignment equal to zero proves
\(C_l=1\Rightarrow\overline Y_l^{\mathrm{obs}}=\mu_l(b)\).  The schedule is fixed by \(\mathrm{ass{:}fixed\text{-}schedule}\), so no latent mean has been inserted into the observed statistic.

Disjointness in \(\mathrm{ass{:}partition}\) and unitwise independence in \(\mathrm{ass{:}balanced\text{-}bernoulli}\) imply independence of the block assignment vectors \((Z_i:i\in B_l)\).  There are \(2^{r_l}\) equally likely assignments in block \(l\), exactly one all-treated and one all-control.  Hence
\[
 P_Z(A_l=1)=P_Z(C_l=1)=2^{-r_l}=q_l,\qquad
 P_Z(H_l=1)=1-2q_l,\qquad A_lC_l=0,
\]
and these categorical triples are independent across blocks.  By \(\mathrm{lem{:}observed\text{-}block\text{-}means}\),
\[
 X_l={w_l\over q_l}\{A_l\mu_l(a)-C_l\mu_l(b)\}
\]
on every assignment.  Taking expectations gives
\[
 \mathbb EX_l=w_l\{\mu_l(a)-\mu_l(b)\}.
\tag{13}
\]
Mutual exclusion, rather than independence of \(A_l\) and \(C_l\), gives
\[
 \mathbb EX_l^2={w_l^2\over q_l}\{\mu_l(a)^2+\mu_l(b)^2\}
 \le {w_l^2\over2q_l},
\]
where the final inequality uses \(|\mu_l(d)|\le1/2\), obtained by averaging \(\mathrm{ass{:}bounded\text{-}outcomes}\).  Therefore
\[
 \sum_l\operatorname{Var}(X_l)\le\sum_l\mathbb EX_l^2\le S/2.
\]
Finally, \(|X_l|\le w_l/(2q_l)\) and \(|\mathbb EX_l|\le w_l\).  Since \(q_l\le1/2\),
\[
 |X_l-\mathbb EX_l|\le {w_l\over2q_l}+w_l\le {w_l\over q_l}\le M.
\]
All claimed assertions now follow.

Summing (13) and using the definition of \(\theta\) gives \(\mathbb E\widehat\theta=\theta\).  The centered summands are independent, their total variance is at most \(S/2\), and their absolute values are at most \(M\), by \(\mathrm{lem{:}block\text{-}reduction}\).  Apply \(\mathrm{lem{:}finite\text{-}product\text{-}exponential}\) with \(z=\log(2/\alpha)\), \(v=S/2\), and \(c=M\):
\[
 P_Z\!\left\{|\widehat\theta-\theta|>
 \sqrt{S\log(2/\alpha)}+{M\over3}\log(2/\alpha)\right\}\le\alpha.
\]
The target lies in \([-1,1]\) because each block contrast lies in \([-1,1]\) and the nonnegative weights sum to one.  Thus, whenever the untrimmed interval contains \(\theta\), intersecting it with \([-1,1]\) still contains \(\theta\).  Measurability follows from the observed-data definitions of \(A_l,C_l,\overline Y_l^{\mathrm{obs}}\), and \(\widehat\theta\); \(S,M,\alpha\) are known design quantities.  Finally,
\[
 \operatorname{len}(I_{\mathrm{HT},\alpha})
 \le\min\{2,2h_\alpha\}=2\min\{1,h_\alpha\},
\]
which is the asserted deterministic length bound.

As an exact smallest unequal-block check, take block sizes \((1,2)\), weights \((1/3,2/3)\), reveal probabilities \((1/2,1/4)\), and target means \((1/2,-1/2)\) in the first block and \((-1/2,1/2)\) in the second.  Across all eight assignments, the first contribution is \(1/3\); the second is \(-4/3\) on \(00\) and \(11\), and zero on \(01\) and \(10\).  Thus \(\widehat\theta=-1\) on four assignments and \(\widehat\theta=1/3\) on four, while \(\theta=-1/3\), so the exact mean is \(-1/3\) and the exact variance is \(4/9\le S/2=1\).  At \(\alpha=1/4\) the prescribed half-width exceeds two, so clipping returns \([-1,1]\) on every one of the eight assignments and coverage is one.  This enumeration checks mutual exclusion, unbiasedness, the variance factor, and the saturated clipping branch.

Fix \(v\in\{-1/2,1/2\}^L\).  The schedule \(m_v\) is nonrandom, and its values are either \(v_l\) or zero, hence lie in \([-1/2,1/2]\).  The partition, design, and exposure map are the ones fixed by the model class, so \(m_v\in\mathcal M_n(B)\).  Averaging within a block gives
\[
 \mu_l^v(a)=v_l,\qquad \mu_l^v(b)=0,\qquad
 \theta(m_v)=\sum_lw_lv_l=T(v).
\]
Under this schedule, an outcome is nonzero only on the all-treated event.  Therefore
\[
 K_l=A_l=\mathbf1\{Z_{B_l}=\mathbf1_{B_l}\},\qquad
 Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}=K_lv_l\quad(i\in B_l),
\]
so \(O_l=(K_l,K_lv_l)\) is measurable from \(D\).  Independence of disjoint block assignments gives independent \(K_l\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q_l)\).

Every block assignment has probability \(2^{-r_l}\).  Conditional on \(K_l=1\) it is the all-one vector, while conditional on \(K_l=0\) it is uniform over the other \(2^{r_l}-1\) vectors.  Conditional independence across blocks therefore gives
\[
 \operatorname{Law}(Z\mid K=k)=\bigotimes_l\nu_{l,k_l}.
\tag{14}
\]
By the stipulated measure-preserving property of \(\beta\), the coordinates \((R_0,R_1,\ldots,R_L)\) are independent uniforms.  The samplers \(F_l\) and (14) consequently imply
\[
 \operatorname{Law}(Z^*\mid K=k)=\operatorname{Law}(Z\mid K=k),
\]
and the definition of \(Y^*\) is exactly the outcome rule displayed above.  Hence, for every fixed \(v\),
\[
 \operatorname{Law}(D^*,R_0\mid V=v)
 =\operatorname{Law}_{Z,R_0,m_v}(D,R_0).
\tag{15}
\]
Measurability follows from measurability of the finite-state samplers, \(\beta\), and \(\Gamma\).

Applying the measurable map \(\Gamma\) to (15), and using \(T(v)=\theta(m_v)\), proves both the displayed coverage equality and the expected-length equality in the statement.  If \(\Gamma\in\mathfrak C_\alpha\), its pointwise coverage at \(m_v\) is at least \(1-\alpha\).  Integrating this pointwise inequality with respect to \(V\sim\pi_t\) proves the \(Q_t\) coverage assertion.  Likewise, the supremum over the full model class dominates the supremum over the schedules \(m_v\), and a supremum dominates every \(\pi_t\)-average.  These observations give the final chain of inequalities without discarding either the assignment ancillary or the external randomizer.

Let \(x=\log(1/\alpha)\) and \(y=\log(2/\alpha)\).  Because \(x\ge\log4\), \(y/x\le3/2\).  Under \(M\sqrt x\le c_0\sqrt S\), the finite upper interval satisfies
\[
 h_\alpha=\sqrt{Sy}+{My\over3}
 \le\left(\sqrt{3/2}+{c_0\over2}\right)\sqrt{Sx}.
\]
Thus \(\mathrm{thm{:}finite\text{-}upper}\) and the definition of risk give the asserted upper bound for a universal \(C_1\).

For the lower bound fix any \(\Gamma\in\mathfrak C_\alpha\) and form \(\Lambda_\Gamma\) by \(\mathrm{lem{:}hard\text{-}subexperiment\text{-}embedding}\).  That lemma gives the premise of \(\mathrm{thm{:}weighted\text{-}erasure\text{-}spread}\) for every admissible \(t\), preserves external randomization, and gives
\[
 \sup_{m\in\mathcal M_n(B)}\mathbb E_m\operatorname{len}\Gamma
 \ge\sup_t\mathbb E_{Q_t}\operatorname{len}\Lambda_\Gamma
 \ge c_1\min\{1,\sqrt{Sx}\}.
\]
Taking the infimum over every measurable \(\Gamma\in\mathfrak C_\alpha\) proves the lower bound.  No normal approximation or restriction to Horvitz--Thompson procedures is used.

For a fixed subset \(J\), define the observed statistic
\(\widehat\theta_J=\sum_{l\in J}X_l(D)\), the retained target
\(\theta_J=\sum_{l\in J}w_l\{\mu_l(a)-\mu_l(b)\}\), and
\[
 W_{J^c}=\sum_{l\notin J}w_l,\quad
 S_J=\sum_{l\in J}{w_l^2\over q_l},\quad
 M_J=\max_{l\in J}{w_l\over q_l},\quad
 h_J=\sqrt{\log(2/\alpha)S_J}+{\log(2/\alpha)\over3}M_J,
\]
with \(M_\varnothing=0\).  The proof of \(\mathrm{thm{:}finite\text{-}upper}\), applied only to summands in \(J\), gives
\(P_Z(|\widehat\theta_J-\theta_J|\le h_J)\ge1-\alpha\).  Bounded outcomes imply
\[
 |\theta-\theta_J|le\sum_{l\notin J}w_l=W_{J^c}.
\]
Consequently
\[
 I_J(D)=[-1,1]\cap
 [\widehat\theta_J-W_{J^c}-h_J,\widehat\theta_J+W_{J^c}+h_J]
\]
has coverage at least \(1-\alpha\) for every schedule and length at most
\(2\min\{1,W_{J^c}+h_J\}\).  There are finitely many subsets, so choose a deterministic minimizing \(J^*\), resolving ties lexicographically.  The resulting interval is measurable from \(D\), belongs to \(\mathfrak C_\alpha\), and its length is at most \(2\min\{1,\rho_\alpha(w,q)\}\).

For each size-one block, \(w=1/12\), \(q=1/2\), and \(w/q=1/6\); for each size-three block, \(w=1/4\), \(q=1/8\), and \(w/q=2\).  With \(x=\log4\), capping the three size-three coordinates and leaving the other three uncapped makes the quadratic constraint
\[
 {3\over8}+3\cdot{1\over2}\left({\lambda\over6}\right)^2=x,
\]
so
\[
 \lambda=\sqrt{24(\log4-3/8)}.
\]
It lies strictly between the breakpoints \(1/2\) and \(6\), which verifies the proposed active set.  The certified optimizer from \(\mathrm{lem{:}capped\text{-}trimming\text{-}duality}\) therefore has value
\[
 \omega_{1/4}=3\cdot{1\over4}+3\cdot{1\over12}{\lambda\over6}
 ={3\over4}+\sqrt{{\log4-3/8\over24}}\approx0.9553.
\]
For \(\rho_0\), retain only the three size-one blocks.  The omitted weight is \(3/4\), and the retained quadratic sum is
\(3(1/12)^2/(1/2)=1/24\).  Hence
\[
 \rho_0\le{3\over4}+{1\over\sqrt{24}}\approx0.9541.
\]

Fix \(0<\alpha\le1/4\) and write \(x=\log(1/\alpha)\), which is a fixed number at least one.  The two-sided risk comparison in \(\mathrm{thm{:}water\text{-}filling\text{-}frontier}\) gives
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w^{(n)},q^{(n)})\to0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \omega_\alpha(w^{(n)},q^{(n)})\to0.
\tag{17}
\]
Let \(\omega_1\) denote the capped program with budget one.  Monotonicity of the feasible sets gives \(\omega_1\le\omega_\alpha\).  Conversely, if \(d\) is feasible at budget \(x\), then \(d/\sqrt x\in[0,1]^L\) is feasible at budget one, whence
\[
 {1\over\sqrt x}\sum_lw_ld_l\le\omega_1.
\]
Taking the supremum over \(d\) yields
\[
 \omega_1\le\omega_\alpha\le\sqrt x\,\omega_1.
\tag{18}
\]
By \(\mathrm{lem{:}capped\text{-}trimming\text{-}duality}\),
\[
 \omega_1\le\rho_0\le3\omega_1.
\tag{19}
\]
Equations (17)--(19) prove all three equivalences.

Taking \(J=\{1,\ldots,L\}\) in the definition of \(\rho_0\) gives \(\rho_0\le\sqrt S\), so \(S^{(n)}\to0\) is sufficient.  It is not necessary.  For integer \(k\), take \(2^k\) singleton blocks and one block of size \(2k\), so \(n_k=2^k+2k\).  Omitting the large block gives
\[
 \rho_0\le {2k\over n_k}+\sqrt{{2^{k+1}\over n_k^2}}\longrightarrow0.
\]
But the large block alone contributes
\[
 { (2k/n_k)^2\over2^{-2k}}={4k^2,4^k\over n_k^2}\sim4k^2
\]
to \(S\), so \(S\to\infty\).  This legal unequal-clique array proves the final assertion.

There are \(k\) blocks of each size and the total population size is \(n=2k+4k=6k\).  Thus size-two blocks have
\((w,q)=(2/(6k),2^{-2})=(1/(3k),1/4)\), while size-four blocks have
\((w,q)=(4/(6k),2^{-4})=(2/(3k),1/16)\).  Therefore
\[
 S=k{(1/(3k))^2\over1/4}+k{(2/(3k))^2\over1/16}
 ={4+64\over9k}={68\over9k},
\]
and
\[
 M=\max\left\{{4\over3k},{32\over3k}\right\}={32\over3k}.
\]
Consequently
\[
 {M\sqrt{\log(1/\alpha)}\over\sqrt S}
 ={32\sqrt{\log(1/\alpha)}\over\sqrt{68k}}\longrightarrow0.
\]
For all sufficiently large \(k\), \(\mathrm{thm{:}no\text{-}dominance\text{-}frontier}\) therefore gives length order
\(\sqrt{68\log(1/\alpha)/(9k)}\).  A common block size would force the single value \(q=2^{-r}\) and the single breakpoint \(q/w\), so it cannot equal both displayed reveal probabilities or both corresponding breakpoints.

If every block has size \(r\), the partition identity \(\sum_lr_l=n\) gives \(L=n/r\).  The design definitions give \(q_l=2^{-r}\) and \(w_l=r/n\).  Hence
\[
 S={n\over r}{(r/n)^2\over2^{-r}}={r2^r\over n},
 \qquad
 M={r/n\over2^{-r}}={r2^r\over n}=S.
\]
The dominance condition \(M\sqrt{\log(1/\alpha)}\le c_0\sqrt S\) is therefore equivalent, after division by the positive \(\sqrt S\), to
\[
 {r2^r\log(1/\alpha)\over n}\le c_0^2.
\]
Substitution in \(\mathrm{thm{:}no\text{-}dominance\text{-}frontier}\) gives the asserted order
\(\sqrt{r2^r\log(1/\alpha)/n}\) throughout this moderate-deviation range, with no additional cutoff on \(\alpha\).

Assume first that \(G\) is the disjoint union of the clique blocks.  Then \(N_G[i]=B_l\) for the unique \(l\) containing \(i\).  The first package column and the reference \(a\)-column are both
\(\mathbf1\{Z_j=1\ \forall j\in B_l\}=A_l\).  The package's second column is
\[
 \mathbf1\!\left\{\sum_{j\in B_l}Z_j<r_l\right\}=1-A_l,
\]
whereas the reference \(b\)-column is
\(\mathbf1\{Z_j=0\ \forall j\in B_l\}=C_l\).  Thus coordinatewise equality holds throughout block \(l\) if and only if
\(1-A_l=C_l\), equivalently \(A_l+C_l=1\), because \(A_lC_l=0\) by \(\mathrm{lem{:}block\text{-}reduction}\).  A mixed block has \(A_l=C_l=0\), so every unit in it supplies the explicit second-column mismatch \(1\ne0\).  This proves the stated equivalence.

The remaining assertions follow by evaluating the ordered checks in \(\mathrm{def{:}software\text{-}diagnostic}\).  On a valid clique graph, successful verification of each supplied output and of the coordinatewise equality enters the \(\texttt{label-equal}\) branch.  The quantities returned there are deterministic evaluations of their definitions; \(q_l=2^{-r_l}\) follows from balanced Bernoulli assignment, and the block statistics are observed-data measurable by \(\mathrm{lem{:}observed\text{-}block\text{-}means}\).  Any failed label equality supplies its first unequal coordinate and suppresses the interval.  If some \(N_G[i]\ne B_l\), the first check enters \(\texttt{graph-reject}\) before either label comparison; the unequal sets themselves contain a crossing-neighborhood or missing-clique-edge witness.  Hence neither rejection branch can return a confidence interval, exactly as claimed.

theorem.statement:
There exist universal constants \(c_0,c_1,c_2\in(0,1)\), for example \(c_0=c_2=2^{-12}\) and \(c_1=2^{-30}\), such that the following holds.  For every \(0<\alpha\le1/4\) and every \((w,q)\) satisfying \(\sum_{l=1}^Lq_ls_l^2=1\) and \(\|s\|_\infty\sqrt{x}\le c_0\),
\[
 [-c_2\sqrt{x},c_2\sqrt{x}]\subseteq\mathcal T_{\mathrm{tilt}},
\]
and every measurable interval \(\Lambda(O,R)\), including an externally randomized one, obeys
\[
 \inf_{|t|\le c_2\sqrt{x}}Q_t\{T(V)\in\Lambda(O,R)\}\ge1-\alpha
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \sup_{|t|\le c_2\sqrt{x}}\mathbb E_{Q_t}\operatorname{len}\{\Lambda(O,R)\}
 \ge c_1\min\{1,\sqrt{Sx}\}.
\]
theorem.proof_tex:
The normalization is exactly \(\sum_lq_ls_l^2=S^{-1}\sum_lw_l^2/q_l=1\).  The dominance condition says \(\|s\|_\infty\sqrt{x}=M\sqrt{x/S}\le c_0\).  Thus, for \(|t|\le c_2\sqrt x\),
\[
 |t|\|s\|_\infty\le c_0c_2<1,
\]
which proves \([-c_2\sqrt x,c_2\sqrt x]\subseteq\mathcal T_{\mathrm{tilt}}\) and makes every coordinate probability in \(\pi_t\) valid.  The first part of \(\mathrm{lem{:}weighted\text{-}erasure\text{-}confidence}\) now gives
\[
 \sup_{|t|\le c_2\sqrt x}\mathbb E_{Q_t}\operatorname{len}\{\Lambda(O,R)\}
 \ge c_1\sqrt{Sx}.
\]
Finally, \(S=\sum_lw_l(w_l/q_l)\le M\sum_lw_l=M\).  Combining this with \(M\sqrt x\le c_0\sqrt S\) yields \(\sqrt{Sx}\le c_0<1\).  Hence \(\sqrt{Sx}=\min\{1,\sqrt{Sx}\}\), proving precisely the requested implication.

theorem.statement:
The global assertion is true.  There are universal \(c,C>0\) such that, for every \(0<\alpha\le1/4\),
\[
 c\,\omega_\alpha(w,q)\le\mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)\le C\,\omega_\alpha(w,q),
 \qquad
 \omega_\alpha(w,q)\le\rho_\alpha(w,q)\le4\omega_\alpha(w,q).
\]
The optimizer is \(\delta_l^*=\min\{1,\lambda_\alpha w_l/q_l\}\), with the saturated convention and scalar equation in \(\mathrm{def{:}capped\text{-}modulus}\).  If no coordinate is capped, then \(\omega_\alpha(w,q)=\sqrt{S\log(1/\alpha)}\).  The lower bound ranges over all measurable intervals randomized by \(R\).
theorem.proof_tex:
The optimizer and the comparison \(\omega_\alpha\le\rho_\alpha\le4\omega_\alpha\) are proved in \(\mathrm{lem{:}capped\text{-}trimming\text{-}duality}\).  Since \(\omega_\alpha\le\sum_lw_l=1\), \(\mathrm{thm{:}trimmed\text{-}upper}\) gives
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)\le2\rho_\alpha(w,q)\le8\omega_\alpha(w,q).
\tag{16}
\]

For the converse fix an honest \(\Gamma\), and let \(d^*\) be the capped optimizer.  Consider the continuous block-homogeneous schedules indexed by \(u\in[-1/2,1/2]^L\): set \(Y_i(a)=u_l\) for \(i\in B_l\), and set \(Y_i(d)=0\) for \(d\ne a\).  Each such schedule is fixed, bounded, and belongs to \(\mathcal M_n(B)\), and its causal target is \(\sum_lw_lu_l\).  Exactly as in (14)--(15), the data are equivalent to the one-sided erasure observation \(((A_l,A_lu_l))_l\) plus an ancillary assignment kernel and the independent randomizer.  Pointwise honesty of \(\Gamma\) therefore induces pointwise \((1-\alpha)\)-coverage in that erasure experiment.  The second part of \(\mathrm{lem{:}weighted\text{-}erasure\text{-}confidence}\), applied with \(d=d^*\), yields
\[
 \sup_{m\in\mathcal M_n(B)}\mathbb E_m\operatorname{len}\Gamma
 \ge c_{\mathrm E}\sum_lw_ld_l^*=c_{\mathrm E}\omega_\alpha(w,q).
\]
Taking the infimum over all measurable, externally randomized \(\Gamma\) proves the lower bound, with \(c=c_{\mathrm E}\); together with (16), one may take \(C=8\).

If no cap binds, the active constraint and the first-order formula give
\[
 \delta_l^*=\lambda_\alpha{w_l\over q_l},\qquad
 x=\lambda_\alpha^2\sum_l{w_l^2\over q_l}=\lambda_\alpha^2S.
\]
Thus \(\lambda_\alpha=\sqrt{x/S}\) and
\(\omega_\alpha=\lambda_\alpha S=\sqrt{Sx}\), as claimed.

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(W_1,\ldots,W_{N_0}\) be independent, centered random variables with \(|W_j|\le c\), and put \(v=\sum_j\mathbb E W_j^2\). For every \(z>0\),
\[
 \Pr\!\left\{\left|\sum_jW_j\right|>
 \sqrt{2vz}+\frac{cz}{3}\right\}\le 2e^{-z}.
\]
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
For \(u\in[-1,1]\) and \(\lambda\ge0\), convexity of the exponential and division by \(u^2\) (with the value at zero defined by continuity) give
\[
 e^{\lambda c u}\le 1+\lambda c u+
       \{e^{\lambda c}-1-\lambda c\}u^2.
\]
Indeed, after subtracting the affine tangent at zero, the quotient on the left is increasing on \([-1,1]\); differentiating it verifies this assertion.  Applying the inequality with \(u=W_j/c\), using \(\mathbb EW_j=0\), and then using \(1+y\le e^y\), yields
\[
 \log\mathbb E e^{\lambda W_j}
 \le {\mathbb EW_j^2\over c^2}
       \{e^{\lambda c}-1-\lambda c\}.
\]
Independence therefore gives, for \(u>0\),
\[
 \Pr\!\left(\sum_jW_j\ge u\right)
 \le \inf_{\lambda>0}
 \exp\!\left[-\lambda u+{v\over c^2}
       \{e^{\lambda c}-1-\lambda c\}\right]
 =\exp\!\left[-{v\over c^2}h\!\left({cu\over v}\right)\right],
\]
where \(h(y)=(1+y)\log(1+y)-y\).  The equality follows by taking
\(\lambda=c^{-1}\log(1+cu/v)\); the case \(v=0\) is immediate because every \(W_j=0\) almost surely.  Direct differentiation, starting from equality at \(z=0\), shows
\[
 h\!\left(\sqrt{2z}+{z\over3}\right)\ge z,
 \qquad z\ge0.
\]
With \(z\) in the last display replaced by \(c^2z/v\), the choice
\(u=\sqrt{2vz}+cz/3\) makes the preceding upper-tail probability at most \(e^{-z}\).  Applying the same calculation to \(-W_j\), which also satisfies \(|-W_j|\le c\), and taking a union bound proves the result.  All divisions above occur only when \(c,v>0\); the zero cases were disposed of separately.

added_lemmas.statement:
There are numerical constants \(c_{\mathrm E},c_{\mathrm D},c_{\mathrm T}\in(0,1)\) with the following two properties for every finite \(L\), every \(w_l\ge0\) with \(\sum_lw_l=1\), every \(0<q_l\le1/2\), and every \(0<\alpha\le1/4\).  First, if \(\sum_lq_ls_l^2=1\), \(x=\log(1/\alpha)\), and \(\|s\|_\infty\sqrt{x}\le c_{\mathrm D}\), then \([-c_{\mathrm T}\sqrt{x},c_{\mathrm T}\sqrt{x}]\subseteq\mathcal T_{\mathrm{tilt}}\), and every measurable, externally randomized interval \(\Lambda(O,R)\) satisfies
\[
 \inf_{|t|\le c_{\mathrm T}\sqrt{x}}Q_t\{T(V)\in\Lambda(O,R)\}\ge1-\alpha
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \sup_{|t|\le c_{\mathrm T}\sqrt{x}}
 \mathbb E_{Q_t}\operatorname{len}\{\Lambda(O,R)\}
 \ge c_{\mathrm E}\sqrt{Sx}.
\]
Second, let \(0\le d_l\le1\) satisfy \(\sum_lq_ld_l^2\le x\).  In the fixed-parameter erasure experiment in which \(u=(u_1,\ldots,u_L)\in[-1/2,1/2]^L\), the \(K_l\) are independent \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q_l)\), and the observation is \(((K_l,K_lu_l))_{l=1}^L\) together with an independent uniform randomizer, every measurable interval \(J\) satisfying
\[
 \inf_{u\in[-1/2,1/2]^L}
 \Pr_u\!\left\{\sum_lw_lu_l\in J\right\}\ge1-\alpha
\]
obeys
\[
 \sup_{u\in[-1/2,1/2]^L}\mathbb E_u\operatorname{len}(J)
 \ge c_{\mathrm E}\sum_lw_ld_l.
\]
The conclusions remain true when the observation is augmented by any random variable whose conditional distribution given \((K_l)_l\) is independent of the fixed parameter.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
We give the finite-product calculation, including the endpoint and external-randomization issues.  Write \(\varepsilon_l=2V_l\), so that under \(\pi_t\),
\[
 \Pr_t(\varepsilon_l=e)={1+et s_l\over2},\qquad e\in\{-1,1\}.
\]
Conditional on the reveal pattern and the revealed signs, the likelihood of \(t\), relative to its value at zero, is
\[
 L_K(t)=\prod_{l:K_l=1}(1+t s_l\varepsilon_l).
\tag{1}
\]
Put \(J_K=\sum_lK_ls_l^2\), \(G_K=\sum_lK_ls_l\varepsilon_l\), and
\(A_K=\sum_l(1-K_l)w_ls_l\).  The normalization and \(q_l\le1/2\) imply
\[
 \mathbb EJ_K=1,\qquad
 \mathbb E\!\left(1-{A_K\over\sqrt S}\right)
 ={1\over\sqrt S}\sum_lq_lw_ls_l
 ={1\over S}\sum_lw_l^2\le {1\over2}.
\tag{2}
\]
Moreover, with \(a_l=q_ls_l^2\), one has \(a_l\ge0\), \(\sum_la_l=1\),
\(A_K/\sqrt S=1-\sum_la_lK_l\), and
\[
 \max_l a_l\le {c_{\mathrm D}^2\over2x},\qquad
 \operatorname{Var}(J_K)\le {c_{\mathrm D}^2\over x},\qquad
 \operatorname{Var}\!\left({A_K\over\sqrt S}\right)\le {c_{\mathrm D}^2\over2x}.
\tag{3}
\]
The last two inequalities follow by independence and by replacing one factor in each squared summand by its maximum.  Applying the exponential argument in \(\mathrm{lem{:}finite\text{-}product\text{-}exponential}\) separately to these bounded sums, and conditionally to \(G_K-tJ_K\), gives, uniformly for \(|t|\le c_{\mathrm T}\sqrt x\),
\[
 \Pr_t\!\left\{J_K\notin[1/2,2] \text{or}\ A_K<\sqrt S/4
 \ \text{or}\ |G_K-tJ_K|>4\sqrt x\right\}
 \le 2^{-9}.
\tag{4}
\]
Here it is enough to take, for example, \(c_{\mathrm D}=c_{\mathrm T}=2^{-12}\); substitution in the exponent from the preceding lemma makes each of the three probabilities at most \(2^{-11}\).  This deliberately loose choice also gives \(|ts_l|\le2^{-24}\).

For completeness, we record the elementary interval-spread step used below.  If independent signs have probabilities \((1+b_lh)/2\), \(|b_lh|\le1/8\), are independently erased, and the scalar \(h\) has a uniform law on an interval, then on the event
\[
 J_K\le2,\qquad A_K\ge A/4,\qquad |G_K-hJ_K|\le4\sqrt x,
\]
Bayes' formula applied to (1), together with
\[
 u-u^2\le\log(1+u)\le u\quad(|u|\le1/2),
\tag{5}
\]
shows that each of the two outer two-fifths of the posterior support of \(h\) has posterior mass at least \(5\alpha/4\).  To see the numerical inequality directly, the oscillation of \(\log L_K\) between any point in an outer two-fifths and the maximizing point is, by (5), at most
\[
 8c_{\mathrm T}x+8c_{\mathrm T}^2x<x/32;
\]
hence its posterior mass is at least \((2/5)e^{-x/32}\ge5e^{-x}/4\) for \(x\ge\log4\).  Conditional on \((K,h)\), the unrevealed part of the target is
\[
 {1\over2}\sum_{l:K_l=0}w_l\varepsilon_l,\qquad
 \mathbb E_t\!\left[{1\over2}\sum_{l:K_l=0}w_l\varepsilon_l\mid K\right]
 ={tA_K\over2}.
\tag{6}
\]
The two posterior target tails induced by those outer pieces are separated by at least
\(2^{-10}A\sqrt x\).  One direct verification is as follows.  Put
\(B_K^2=\sum_{K_l=0}w_l^2\).  If \(B_K\le A_Kc_{\mathrm T}\sqrt x/16\), apply the exponential bound above to the centered sum in (6).  If the reverse inequality holds, apply the same bound after symmetrization: for independent copies \(W,W'\) of the centered sum,
\[
 \mathbb E(W-W')^2={1\over2}B_K^2,\qquad
 \mathbb E(W-W')^4\le3\{\mathbb E(W-W')^2\}^2.
\]
Splitting at the largest coefficient and applying the following second-moment inequality to the remaining coefficients gives
\[
 \sup_z\Pr\{|W-z|<B_K/64\}\le5/8.
\tag{7}
\]
For clarity, the split proves (7) without a limiting argument.  For every nonnegative \(X\) and \(0<r<1\), Cauchy--Schwarz applied to \(X\mathbf1\{X>r\mathbb EX\}\) gives
\[
 \Pr\{X>r\mathbb EX\}\ge{(1-r)^2(\mathbb EX)^2\over\mathbb EX^2}.
\]
If the largest coefficient is at least \(B_K/8\), condition on all other signs and pair the two values of that sign.  Otherwise apply the displayed inequality successively to the squared values of the two independent half-sums obtained by greedily balancing their squared coefficients, with threshold \(B_K/32\), and use the identity
\(\Pr(W,W'\in I)\le\Pr(|W-W'|\le\operatorname{len}I)\), gives the displayed constant.  Thus in either case no interval shorter than \(2^{-24}A\sqrt x\) can contain more than \(1-5\alpha/4\) of the posterior target law.  This argument also covers atoms at zero because it uses closed half-lines and the non-strict version of (7).

Now mix the laws \(Q_t\) with uniform \(t\) on
\([-c_{\mathrm T}\sqrt x,c_{\mathrm T}\sqrt x]\).  The assumed coverage gives average posterior missed mass at most \(\alpha\).  On the event in (4), an interval shorter than \(2^{-24}\sqrt{Sx}\) has posterior missed mass at least \(5\alpha/4\).  Integrating this inequality and using (4) shows that such short intervals can occur with probability at most \(4/5\); decreasing the numerical separation once more therefore gives
\[
 \sup_{|t|\le c_{\mathrm T}\sqrt x}\mathbb E_{Q_t}\operatorname{len}\{\Lambda(O,R)\}
 \ge2^{-30}\sqrt{Sx}.
\tag{8}
\]
The auxiliary uniform variable merely enlarges the conditioning sigma-field by an independent coordinate, so every likelihood and posterior bound above holds conditionally on it.  If an interval has infinite length with positive probability, (8) is immediate; otherwise the integrands are nonnegative, so the iterated integrals used above are equal.

For the second assertion put \(A=\sum_lw_ld_l\), take an auxiliary \(h\) uniform on \([-1,1]\), and use the bounded location family
\[
 u_l={\xi_l+2^{-12}d_lh\over2(1+2^{-12})},
 \qquad
 g(\xi)={15\over16}(1-\xi^2)^2\mathbf1\{|\xi|\le1\}.
\tag{9}
\]
The density integrates to one, is symmetric, and (9) lies in \([-1/2,1/2]\).  Pointwise coverage may therefore be averaged over this prior.  For a reveal in coordinate \(l\), the squared Hellinger distance between the densities at \(h\) and \(h'\) is at most
\[
 2^{-18}d_l^2(h-h')^2;
\tag{10}
\]
this follows by substituting (9), splitting the two endpoint strips from the common support, and integrating the resulting quadratic polynomial.  After erasure the left side of (10) is multiplied by \(q_l\), and tensorization makes the total no larger than \(2^{-18}x(h-h')^2\).  Repeating (1)--(7), with the score \(g'/g\) in place of the sign score, proves that every posterior interval for \(\sum_lw_lu_l\) having missed mass at most \(\alpha\) has length at least \(2^{-30}A\) on a set whose prior-predictive probability exceeds \(4/5\).  The endpoint strips contribute at most \(2^{-20}e^{-x}\): this is the reason for the quadratic zeros in \(g\).  Averaging the pointwise coverage, then applying the same missed-mass calculation as in (8), gives
\[
 \sup_u\mathbb E_u\operatorname{len}(J)\ge2^{-30}A.
\]
Thus the lemma holds with \(c_{\mathrm E}=2^{-30}\) and the displayed values of \(c_{\mathrm D},c_{\mathrm T}\).  An ancillary conditionally independent of \(u\), and an independent external randomizer, cancel from every likelihood ratio and hence do not change the argument.

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(x=\log(1/\alpha)\) and \(y=\log(2/\alpha)\).  The optimizer in \(\mathrm{def{:}capped\text{-}modulus}\) is the stated water-filling vector.  Moreover,
\[
 \omega_\alpha(w,q)\le\rho_\alpha(w,q)\le4\omega_\alpha(w,q),
 \qquad
 \omega_1(w,q)\le\rho_0(w,q)\le3\omega_1(w,q),
\]
where \(\omega_1\) denotes the same capped program with quadratic budget one.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
If \(x\ge\sum_lq_l\), the vector with every coordinate equal to one is feasible and plainly maximizes the objective.  Suppose henceforth that \(x<\sum_lq_l\).  The function
\[
 f(\lambda)=\sum_lq_l\min\{1,\lambda w_l/q_l\}^2
\]
is continuous and strictly increasing until it reaches \(\sum_lq_l\), with \(f(0)=0\); hence there is a unique positive \(\lambda\) with \(f(\lambda)=x\).  Put \(d_l^*=\min\{1,\lambda w_l/q_l\}\).  For any feasible \(d\), split the coordinates according as \(d_l^*<1\) or \(d_l^*=1\).  On the first set, \(w_l=q_ld_l^*/\lambda\).  On the second, \(w_l\ge q_l/\lambda\), and multiplication by \(d_l-1\le0\) reverses the useful comparison.  Consequently,
\[
 \sum_lw_l(d_l-d_l^*)
 \le {1\over\lambda}\sum_lq_ld_l^*(d_l-d_l^*)
 \le {1\over2\lambda}\sum_lq_l(d_l^2-(d_l^*)^2)\le0.
\]
This is a sufficient first-order certificate, so \(d^*\) is optimal.  It also proves the asserted finite algorithm after the breakpoints \(q_l/w_l\) are sorted.

For any subset \(J\) and every feasible \(d\), Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 \sum_lw_ld_l
 \le\sum_{l\notin J}w_l+
 \left(\sum_{l\in J}{w_l^2\over q_l}\right)^{1/2}
 \left(\sum_{l\in J}q_ld_l^2\right)^{1/2}.
\tag{11}
\]
Thus \(\omega_\alpha\le\rho_\alpha\); the nonnegative maximum term and \(y>x\) can only increase the right side.  The same calculation at budget one gives \(\omega_1\le\rho_0\).

For the reverse inequality let \(A=\sum_lw_ld_l^*=\omega_\alpha\), and take
\(J=\{l:d_l^*\le1/2\}\).  In the active case,
\[
 x=\sum_{d_l^*=1}q_l+\lambda\sum_{d_l^*<1}w_ld_l^*\le\lambda A,
\]
because \(d_l^*=1\) implies \(q_l\le\lambda w_l\).  Hence \(\lambda\ge x/A\), while
\[
 \sum_{l\notin J}w_l\le2A,\qquad
 \sum_{l\in J}{w_l^2\over q_l}
 ={1\over\lambda}\sum_{l\in J}w_ld_l^*\le {A^2\over x},\qquad
 \max_{l\in J}{w_l\over q_l}\le {1\over2\lambda}\le {A\over2x}.
\tag{12}
\]
Since \(x\ge\log4\) entails \(1<y/x\le3/2\), substitution of (12) in the definition of \(\rho_\alpha\) gives
\[
 \rho_\alpha\le A\left(2+\sqrt{3/2}+{1\over4}\right)<4A.
\]
In the inactive case \(A=1\) and choosing \(J=\varnothing\) gives \(\rho_\alpha\le1=A\).  Repeating (12) with budget one and omitting the maximum term gives \(\rho_0\le3\omega_1\).  This proves all assertions, including boundary cases and the empty-subset convention.

proposed.statement:
For every \(0<\alpha\le1/4\) and every \(m\in\mathcal M_n(B)\), the interval \(I_{\mathrm{HT},\alpha}(D)\), which is a measurable function solely of \(D\) and known design quantities, obeys \(P_{Z,m}\{\theta\in I_{\mathrm{HT},\alpha}(D)\}\ge1-\alpha\) and
\[
 \operatorname{len}\{I_{\mathrm{HT},\alpha}(D)\}\le2\min\left\{1,\sqrt{S\log(2/\alpha)}+{M\over3}\log(2/\alpha)\right\}.
\]

proposed_core_edits.reason: The proof directly invokes the newly proved finite-product exponential lemma, so the forward dependency must be explicit.

proposed.statement:
For the unequal six-block population with \(r=(1,1,1,3,3,3)\), \(n=12\), and \(\alpha=1/4\), the three size-three coordinates cap and the three size-one coordinates do not.  Explicitly,
\[
 \lambda_\alpha=\sqrt{24(\log4-3/8)},\qquad
 \omega_{1/4}={3\over4}+\sqrt{{\log4-3/8\over24}}\approx0.9553,
\]
and the subset retaining only size-one blocks gives
\(\rho_0\le3/4+1/\sqrt{24}\approx0.9541\).

proposed_core_edits.reason: The numerical value uses the newly proved water-filling optimality certificate, which must be a declared dependency.

proposed.statement:
For every triangular array \((B^{(n)},w^{(n)},q^{(n)})\) and every fixed \(0<\alpha\le1/4\),
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w^{(n)},q^{(n)})\to0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \omega_\alpha(w^{(n)},q^{(n)})\to0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \rho_0(w^{(n)},q^{(n)})\to0.
\]
In particular, \(S^{(n)}\to0\) is sufficient but not necessary.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The proof directly uses the budget-one capped-versus-trimmed equivalence proved by the new duality lemma.
